title: TCP multiplexing and proxy connection reuse — latency sketch
content:
Purpose:

Quick experiment log and reasoning about whether adding a lightweight TCP-level multiplexing layer (connection pooling + request pipelining) in the edge proxy buys latency wins for small-chunk streaming workloads (chat tokens, low-throughput interactive requests) vs using HTTP/2 / gRPC multiplexing alone. This is an exploratory note — not final conclusions.

Background / motivating observations (from prod traces):
- We see a non-negligible tail of first-token latency for short sessions that open a fresh backend connection (particularly from Dedicated hosts behind our HA proxy).
- TLS handshake + TCP handshake + proxy internal allocs currently dominate on p95 for requests under 150 tokens.
- HTTP/2 streams collapse some overhead, but head-of-line blocking on TCP and suboptimal socket reuse patterns in the proxy sometimes negate benefits.

Hypothesis:
- Aggressive connection reuse (long-lived pooled TCP/TLS connections to backends) plus lightweight multiplexing at the proxy (reusing a single socket for single-stream requests without HTTP/2 framing when possible) could cut median/faster-tail latency for small streaming workloads.
- Conversely, mixing multiple concurrent streaming streams on the same TCP connection (true multiplexing) can increase queuing and amplify pauses (KV cache thrash / Nagle + delayed ACKs) for other streams. We need to measure the trade-off.

Experiment matrix (what I ran):
- Testbed: local k8s cluster with simulated backend model-server (v0.9) that emits tokens at configurable pacing. Proxy under test: our in-house edge-proxy (edge-proxy-local) plus a control variant using envoy (v1.23) for baseline.
- Workloads: small-chat (20 tokens, 12ms/token), mid-chat (150 tokens, 8ms/token), large-chat (600 tokens, 5ms/token).
- Concurrency modes: single-stream-per-conn (pool of 50 conns, no multiplex), http2-mux (HTTP/2 streams over shared conn), tcp-pipeline-mux (custom: pool of 10 long-lived TLS connections; proxy interleaves frames at app-level to avoid HTTP/2 overhead, essentially piggyback small messages), mixed (randomly pick one of above per request).
- Network conditions: ideal LAN, 10ms RTT emulated, 40ms RTT emulated, 3% packet loss emulated (tc/netem).
- Metrics: first-byte latency, tail 95/99 for first-byte, overall completion latency, CPU on proxy, connection churn, socket queue depths, number of TLS handshakes per minute.

Key results (observed medians / p95 / qualitative notes):
- Baseline (edge-proxy default small pool 5 conns per backend): first-byte median 42ms, p95 210ms on 10ms RTT.
- Single-stream-per-conn (pool 50): median 28ms, p95 120ms. Connection churn reduced TLS handshakes by ~78% and decreased CPU per-request for TLS setup, but increased total socket count and memory footprint on proxy.
- HTTP/2-mux: median 30ms, p95 190ms. Good median but p95 worse than large pool. Observed stalls when one stream delayed (backpressure from large responses) caused other streams to see spikes due to TCP level queuing and proxy internal serialization chunks.
- TCP-pipeline-mux (10 conns): median 26ms, p95 95ms in ideal network. Under 40ms RTT, p95 jumped to 260ms when concurrent streams hit >20 per connection — likely head-of-line amplification + Nagle interactions.
- Under 3% packet loss, multiplexed modes (HTTP/2 and tcp-pipeline) suffered significantly worse tails compared to single-stream-per-conn; single-stream isolation contained loss impact.

Tracer/observability notes (how we saw the above):
- Added short spans around socket write + backend read in the proxy; correlated with kernel tcp_info to see cwnd/rcv-ssthresh patterns.
- Kernel-level retransmits and retransmit timers dominated the extra latency in loss cases for multiplexed connections.
- TLS resumption (session tickets) helped but didn’t fully eliminate TCP handshake costs at scale where SNI routing pinned to different backends.

Operational trade-offs:
- Single-stream-per-conn: simplest to reason about, best tail under lossy networks, but scales worse in terms of sockets and TLS memory and requires more aggressive connection pooling heuristics to avoid exhaustion.
- Multiplexing (HTTP/2 or TCP-level): better median in ideal networks and lower socket overhead, but risk of H-O-L amplification and worse p95 under loss or when a few heavy streams exist. Needs careful scheduling / circuit breaking per-stream.
- Hybrid seems promising: maintain a small number of long-lived pooled conns (to reduce TLS churn), but prefer single active streaming request per connection for low-latency small requests. Allow true multiplexing only for long-lived high-throughput streams (e.g., embedding batches).

Ideas for next steps / mitigations to prototype:
1) Idle-connection warm pool + probabilistic connection pinning (for customers with consistent backends) — reduces handshakes without exploding socket counts.
2) Per-connection scheduler inside proxy: permit only N concurrent streaming writes per conn; others routed to different conns or backpressured earlier.
3) TCP stack tunables: disable Nagle for streaming sockets, tune delayed ACK heuristics, tune retransmit backoff for short-lived flows (but be careful — TCP tunables can have system-wide effects).
4) QUIC experiment: because QUIC is message-multiplexed and avoids TCP H-O-L, test if it gives both low medians and resilient tails under loss. (Quick note: requires backend model-servers to support --quic or a QUIC edge).
5) Flow-control backpressure signals at application layer — small early-window quotas to avoid head-of-line amplification from a single noisy stream.

Open questions / unknowns:
- For Dedicated tenants with predictable traffic, can we auto-classify traffic (interactive vs bulk) and apply different connection strategies transparently?
- What's the cost curve (ops + resource) if we move to single-stream-per-conn at scale for peak QPS 200k? Rough estimate: socket counts x average lifetime -> need careful capacity planning.
- Are there kernel-level optimizations (SO_PRIORITY, BPF-based egress shaping) that can reduce observed tail without changing app-level multiplexing?

Quick action items (owners):
- Prototype per-connection scheduler in edge-proxy: Mei to spike (SRV-1248). Due: 2 weeks.
- Run QUIC pilot with a small internal model: Liam to coordinate with backend team; create canary in us-west1. Due: 3 weeks.
- Cost modeling for socket explosion: Ravi to run capacity sims and update cost/infra estimates. Due: 1 week.

Notes to self / scratchpad (loose):
- When describing results internally, highlight where multiplexing helps (median under clean nets) vs where it hurts (tail under loss).
- Keep experiment configs and raw traces in GHA with tag bench-tcp-mux-2025-10.
- Might be worth an internal doc/presentation comparing QUIC vs TCP mux for our specific streaming patterns.

References / links (in case someone else wants to reproduce):
- GH: actions/serving-runtime/bench/tcp-mux (workflow + scripts)
- Confluence: dev-notes/networking/multiplexing-brief (draft)
- Kernel tools used: tc (netem), ss, tcpdump, perf, small bpf programs for tcp_info snapshotting

End of note.
